title: King Vision Pay Per View, Ltd. v. J.C. Dimitri’s Restaurant, Inc.
lead: Defendants try to avoid admitting or denying allegations by demanding strict proof; the judge treats the defective responses as admissions under the historical rule.

actors.name: King Vision Pay Per View
actors.role: Plaintiff whose complaint required an answer.

actors.name: J.C. Dimitri’s Restaurant and James Chelios
actors.role: Defendants who answered with a recurring nonresponse.

proceedings: The Northern District of Illinois examined the answer on its own initiative.
It directed the case to proceed with affected allegations admitted, subject to the damages exception.
limits: This pleading order neither awards damages nor finally adjudicates the underlying claim. It uses historical Rule 8(d) numbering and does not address later plausibility doctrine.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: An answer demands proof while avoiding admission or denial
sections.cue: What concrete conduct brought the matter before the judge?
paragraphs: King Vision Pay Per View sued J.C. Dimitri’s Restaurant and James Chelios in federal district court in northern Illinois. The defendants filed a thirty-five-paragraph response, repeatedly saying they neither admitted nor denied the allegations and demanding strict proof.

Senior District Judge Shadur examined that pleading on his own initiative. He counted thirty affected paragraphs, including material incorporated by reference. Direct uses appeared in paragraphs 6–12, 17, 25–26 and 33–34, with incorporation in paragraphs 19 and 28. The opinion focused on these responses and did not develop the underlying commercial events.

sections.title: The judge explains the permitted ways to respond
sections.cue: Why did the strict-proof formula fail?
paragraphs: Rule 8(b) permitted admission, denial, or a statement that the defendant lacked knowledge or information sufficient to form a belief about the allegation’s truth. The last response operated as a denial when made with the objective and subjective good faith required by Rule 11.

The defendants’ formula did none of those things. It did not represent a genuine lack of sufficient knowledge or information. A plaintiff’s ordinary burden to prove contested facts did not create a fourth response option, and a demand for strict proof did not itself put the allegation in dispute.

sources.pinpoint: 333 and note 3; authorized responses and rejected formula

sections.title: Repeated educational efforts lead the judge to apply the rule’s consequence
sections.cue: Why did he not simply request a corrected answer?
paragraphs: Shadur explained that he had encountered this defect for years and had addressed it through orders, published opinions and educational programs. His earlier Gilbert decision was one such treatment. The notes emphasized how easy compliance was, the uncertain origin of the strict-proof formula and the limits of repeated instruction.

Those observations explained his choice to apply the admission consequence here. They did not create a prerequisite that these defendants personally must have received an earlier warning. The rule’s clarity, he added, mattered more than how many supporting cases could be cited.

sources.pinpoint: 333–334 and notes 1–5; reason for applying the consequence

sections.title: The affected allegations are admitted and the lawsuit continues
sections.cue: What did the order leave unresolved?
paragraphs: Historical Rule 8(d) treated allegations requiring an answer as admitted if not denied, except allegations about the amount of damages. On June 17, 1998, Shadur applied that provision to the improper responses and directed the action to proceed on that basis.

His warning of similar treatment for future violations did not impose a monetary sanction. The order was not a final damages judgment or a resolution of every part of King Vision’s claim, and no separate opinion was reported. Later cases concerning pleading plausibility were not part of this decision.

sources.pinpoint: 334; operative order, damages exception and historical scope
